verses.text: Moreover Elihu answered,
“Hear my words, you wise men. Give ear to me, you who have knowledge.
For the ear tries words, as the palate tastes food.
Let us choose for us that which is right. Let us know among ourselves what is good.
For Job has said, ‘I am righteous, God has taken away my right:
Notwithstanding my right I am considered a liar. My wound is incurable, though I am without disobedience.’
What man is like Job, who drinks scorn like water,
Who goes in company with the workers of iniquity, and walks with wicked men?
For he has said, ‘It profits a man nothing that he should delight himself with God.’
“Therefore listen to me, you men of understanding: far be it from God, that he should do wickedness, from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity.
For the work of a man he will render to him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.
Yes surely, God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert justice.
Who put him in charge of the earth? or who has appointed him over the whole world?
If he set his heart on himself, If he gathered to himself his spirit and his breath,
all flesh would perish together, and man would turn again to dust.
“If now you have understanding, hear this. Listen to the voice of my words.
Shall even one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty? —
Who says to a king, ‘Vile!’ or to nobles, ‘Wicked!’?
Who doesn’t respect the persons of princes, nor respects the rich more than the poor; for they all are the work of his hands.
In a moment they die, even at midnight. The people are shaken and pass away. The mighty are taken away without a hand.
“For his eyes are on the ways of a man. He sees all his goings.
There is no darkness, nor thick gloom, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.
For he doesn’t need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.
He breaks in pieces mighty men in ways past finding out, and sets others in their place.
Therefore he takes knowledge of their works. He overturns them in the night, so that they are destroyed.
He strikes them as wicked men in the open sight of others;
because they turned aside from following him, and wouldn’t pay attention to any of his ways,
so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him. He heard the cry of the afflicted.
When he gives quietness, who then can condemn? When he hides his face, who then can see him? Alike whether to a nation, or to a man,
that the godless man may not reign, that there be no one to ensnare the people.
“For has any said to God, ‘I am guilty, but I will not offend any more.
Teach me that which I don’t see. If I have done iniquity, I will do it no more’?
Shall his recompense be as you desire, that you refuse it? For you must choose, and not I. Therefore speak what you know.
Men of understanding will tell me, yes, every wise man who hears me:
‘Job speaks without knowledge. His words are without wisdom.’
I wish that Job were tried to the end, because of his answering like wicked men.
For he adds rebellion to his sin. He claps his hands among us, and multiplies his words against God.”

footnotes.content: A young man steps forward with certainty—Elihu breaks his silence to set Job right. How many of us have sat with someone in pain, burning to explain why their suffering *must* make sense? The Lord knows our hearts mean well, yet sometimes we rush to defend Him before we listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu appeals to reason itself—as if wisdom and truth can be sorted like wheat from chaff. There's something almost touching about his trust that honest minds will agree. Yet I've learned the hardest truths aren't grasped by the ear alone; they settle in the heart only when loss has changed us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mouth tastes; the ear discerns—a folk wisdom about how we test what's true. But notice: just as food can nourish or poison, words can heal or wound. When you've suffered, even true words can land like ash without love behind them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu proposes they *choose together* what's right. Noble, but I've noticed the Lord doesn't consult our committee before acting. His justice moves beyond what we agree is 'good'—it reaches toward redemption in ways we can't foresee.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu quotes Job's pain as doctrine: 'God has taken from me my righteousness.' How this echoes across the centuries—the accusation that God is unjust, that faithfulness goes unrewarded. But accusation and abandonment are two different things; the Lord sees what we cannot.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job insists he's blameless yet lies 'wounded, incurable.' There's a kind of courage in refusing to confess sins he didn't commit—yet pride can look just like integrity. The healing we seek through our own vindication rarely comes; only through humility before the One who sees all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu mocks Job's despair as if it were vice. 'He drinks scorn like water'—there's something almost cruel in the image. I've learned that judgment uttered in the name of correction often wounds most deeply because it claims authority it doesn't possess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By questioning God, Elihu groups Job with 'workers of iniquity'—the logic: only the wicked doubt. But the righteous have always wrestled with the Lord. Abraham questioned; Moses questioned; even Jesus cried out from the cross. Faith isn't blind obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu reports Job's despair: 'It profits nothing to delight in God.' This cuts to the heart—when suffering strips away all earthly reward, does faith itself survive? Yes, I've seen it. The deepest faith comes not from transaction but from recognizing the Giver is better than the gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu affirms what he's about to defend: God cannot do wrong. This is the axiom on which his argument rests. Yet sometimes the Lord permits what confounds our logic—not because He's weak, but because His mercy works in time we cannot see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The law of consequence: a man receives according to his ways. Elihu states it as absolute. Yet the Gospel breaks this symmetry—grace is precisely the reversal of what we deserve. Job's sufferer, and Job the book, both point toward that deeper truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu repeats it: God is just, never unjust. The young man needs to say it again, as if saying it aloud will settle it. But sometimes the only answer to suffering isn't doctrine—it's presence, waiting with someone until they can taste the presence of One who never abandons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who appointed God to govern? No one—His rule is inherent, not delegated. There's freedom in that; we don't govern the universe by our understanding. The relief comes when we stop trying to manage what was never ours to manage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If God withdrew His heart and breath—a moment of contemplation about what holds all things. The thought is dizzying, meant to awe us into silence. But silence before the mystery of His sustaining power is different from silence that refuses to question.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All flesh would perish; dust returns to dust. Memento mori—remember you are mortal. Perhaps in recognizing our fragility, we come closer to receiving grace. The strong in their own sight cannot be healed; only the broken find the Lord meeting them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu presses again: 'Now listen.' There's an almost desperate quality to his repetition. He wants Job to hear, to *understand*. But understanding isn't argument—it's a gift that comes in God's time, often wrapped in suffering itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can one who hates justice rule? Elihu appeals to reason. Yet history shows the wicked often prosper, while the just suffer—until the Last Day. The vindication we need may not come in this life; it comes in the One who rose and will make all things new.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who dares call a king 'vile,' a noble 'wicked'? The question assumes hierarchy, deference. Yet the prophets did exactly that—spoke truth to power in God's name. Elihu's logic here serves order, but the kingdom of God often overturns what earth calls 'order.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God shows no partiality—prince and pauper are equally His work. There's comfort in this for the poor, threat to the powerful. But all are equally in need of grace, equally unable to earn His favor. This alone is justice that endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In a moment, at midnight, the mighty fall without a hand—sudden reversal. The image is meant to show God's power over even the strongest. Yet I've noticed the Lord often waits, gives space for repentance, rather than striking sudden blows. His justice isn't hurried.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His eyes trace all a man's footsteps; He sees every going. Meant to terrify the wicked, this verse can also comfort—He sees you wholly, knows your name, watches where you stumble. Nothing escapes His notice, not even a sparrow's fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No darkness hides the wicked from Him. Elihu's argument: judgment is sure. Yet the hiding we most need isn't from God but *in* God—to be found in Christ where the Father sees us covered in righteousness not our own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He needn't consider a man's plea before judgment—omniscience removes the need for Job's courtroom defense. But here's where Elihu and truth diverge: the Lord *does* hear; He *does* listen. His trial of Job will end in restoration, not condemnation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shatters the mighty in ways past searching out, replaces them with others. History is littered with empires that thought themselves eternal. Only one Kingdom stands forever—built not on force but on the conquered love of a Savior.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He takes knowledge of their works; He overturns them by night. The surveillance is total, the judgment swift in Elihu's telling. Yet God's overturning often comes slowly, hidden within the grain of history, visible only to faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He strikes them openly as wicked men for all to see. Public shame as God's weapon—Elihu wants justice to be visible, undeniable. But the Lord's deepest work is often invisible, personal, internal, healing us where no one else sees.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They turned from following Him; they wouldn't heed His ways. The cause-and-effect: disobedience brings destruction. True enough—yet how often the righteous stumble? The answer isn't blame but grace that lifts us when we fall.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poor cry out to Him; He hears the afflicted. Tucked here: the Lord *does* listen. He heard Job. He hears us. Not with indifference or delay but as a Father who leans close to hear His child's whisper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When He gives quietness, who judges? When He hides His face, who can see? A prayer hidden in Elihu's argument—the desire for that quietness, that rest. Yet God's presence is more precious even than His gifts; in losing His face, we lose everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That the godless don't reign, ensnaring the people—a prayer for righteous rule. We long for it; creation groans for it. But Christ's Kingdom comes through suffering service, not through the removal of evil rulers but through their transformation by His love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Has anyone said to God, 'I am guilty, yet will offend no more'? Elihu poses the question to shame Job. Yet this is exactly what repentance means—to turn, to speak our guilt before Him, to receive grace. Job does this; we all must.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Teach me what I don't see; if I have sinned, I will sin no more.' A sinner's prayer. The irony: Elihu quotes this as a challenge to Job, yet this very prayer is what opens the door to the Lord's mercy—true contrition seeking His instruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Should his recompense match your desire, since you refuse His way? Elihu turns the tables—Job has no say in justice. Yet the deepest grace is that the recompense we deserve *has* been paid by Christ; we receive what we didn't earn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men of understanding will tell me—Elihu appeals to consensus, to the wise. But wisdom doesn't come from the numbers of those who agree; it comes from one who knows the depths of your heart and loves you still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Job speaks without knowledge; his words lack wisdom.' The final condemnation from Elihu—harsh, certain. Yet the book of Job itself contradicts this judgment. God will come to affirm Job's wrestle and rebuke Elihu's eloquence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elihu wishes Job were tested to the end for 'answering like the wicked.' There's a cruelty masked as concern—the wish for more suffering to teach a lesson. But healing comes through grace, not through the grinding wheel of God's judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands against God. Elihu's final jab—yet readers today hear an echo of our own temptation: when tired of silence, when desperate for answers, to add defiance to our grief. The Lord knows; He comes to quiet our clenched fists and hold our trembling hands instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
